statement: In a US household survey, Australian twins and international survey analyses, a younger recalled start was associated with more lifetime drug problems or with dependence onset. The US analysis used DSM-IV diagnoses; the twins used modified drug-problem criteria and did not date when problems began. These designs do not establish that starting young itself causes later problems. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected people took part), 6,447 people (15.6%, weighted) had used drugs from any of ten classes, other than as prescribed, at least 12 times; 18.6% of them had had lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence and 20.1% drug abuse without dependence. Lifetime dependence criteria were met by 33.6% of those who recalled first using drugs at 13 or younger, 26.8% at 14, 25.4% at 15, 17.7% at 16 and between 11.4% and 15.1% at 17 or older (13.6% at 21 or older); abuse without dependence was 28.9% for onset at 13 or younger and 13.6% at 20, with intervening rises as well as falls. After adjustment for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current or former use, the odds of lifetime dependence were about 4% lower, and of abuse about 5% lower, for each later year of first use (coefficients −0.04 and −0.05, SE 0.01; the abstract gives the two the other way round). The age of first use was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses; the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked; family history of drug problems was not measured; conduct problems and other psychiatric disorders were not adjusted for, without establishing whether the survey measured them; current or former use, one of the adjustments, may itself follow from the disorder; and the only prospective study of age at first use and later drug problems the authors discuss, which followed 15-year-old boys for 13 years, found that age at first use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, a result they discount (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate measure). The authors call early onset a powerful predictor, but ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors lowers the risk, and call for prospective studies (Grant & Dawson, 1998). In the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; telephone interviews in 1996–2000 at a median age of 30; both twins took part in 69% of pairs), in 311 same-sex pairs in which one twin recalled first using cannabis before 17 and the co-twin did not (136 identical and 175 fraternal pairs; 234 co-twins started later and 77 never used cannabis), the twin who started early more often met the study’s modified criteria for any illicit drug abuse or dependence (47.6% against 32.8%; conditional odds ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.30), cannabis abuse or dependence (45.7% against 31.8%; 2.13, 1.45 to 3.13), alcohol dependence (42.8% against 29.6%; 2.17, 1.46 to 3.24) and use of other drug classes (2.57 to 5.15). Adjustment for differences between co-twins in early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, depression and social anxiety lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (any drug abuse or dependence 1.98, 1.26 to 3.10; alcohol dependence 1.85, 1.21 to 2.83). The pair comparison controls shared rearing. Some other differences were assessed retrospectively, but peer affiliation was not measured. Identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, so the reported estimates control genetic differences only partly; separate identical-pair estimates were not printed, and 311 of the 407 discordant pairs counted in the paper's concordance analysis were analysed, without explanation. The authors read the results as consistent with a causal role and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). In the 17-survey WHO World Mental Health programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), pooled dependence models compared people who had used each drug. Drug dependence was not assessed in six of those surveys; the analyses therefore do not all cover 17 countries. A later start went with lower odds of dependence; the reported range across all dependence outcomes also includes alcohol and tobacco, and using more drug classes with higher odds, while starting drugs in an unusual order was largely unrelated to dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later? The studies found an association, but do not show that starting young is the cause; some did not date when drug problems began. In a 1992 US survey of adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 of those who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs at some time, against about 1 in 7 of those who started at 21 or older. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often met the study’s drug-problem criteria at some time in life than the twin who did not (about 48 in 100 against 33 in 100). The comparison accounts for growing up in the same home, but other differences between twins, such as friends, could still matter, and the study did not show results for identical twins separately. International surveys also linked a younger start with dependence; drug-dependence analyses covered only the countries that collected those data. All these studies asked adults to remember when they started.
magnitude: Grant & Dawson (1998), people who had used drugs at least 12 times, weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence by recalled age at first drug use (SE): 13 or younger 33.6% (1.9); 14, 26.8% (2.4); 15, 25.4% (1.9); 16, 17.7% (1.3); 17, 15.1% (1.4); 18, 15.0% (1.5); 19, 13.4% (1.9); 20, 11.4% (1.8); 21 or older 13.6% (1.2); abuse without dependence 28.9% (1.9) at 13 or younger to 13.6% (2.0) at 20 (the 11.1% printed for 21 or older is lower than all four subgroup values and is not used); adjusted coefficient per later year of first use −0.04 (SE 0.01) for dependence and −0.05 (0.01) for abuse, odds ratios about 0.96 and 0.95 per year (editors' conversion on the study card); overall, lifetime dependence 18.6% (0.6) and abuse 20.1% (0.6). Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio (95% CI), unadjusted; adjusted: any drug abuse or dependence 47.6% vs 32.8%, 2.24 (1.52–3.30); 1.98 (1.26–3.10); cannabis abuse or dependence 45.7% vs 31.8%, 2.13 (1.45–3.13); 1.96 (1.25–3.09); alcohol dependence 42.8% vs 29.6%, 2.17 (1.46–3.24); 1.85 (1.21–2.83); use of sedatives 2.83, hallucinogens 5.15, cocaine or other stimulants 4.19, opioids 2.57 (unadjusted). Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010): pooled dependence-onset models among people who had used each drug; drug dependence not assessed in six of the programme’s 17 surveys. Later onset was associated with lower odds. The 0.2–0.7 range across all outcomes includes alcohol and tobacco and is not a drug-dependence-only range; unit not stated.

risk_of_bias.note: In both main studies the age of first use and the lifetime diagnoses were reported at the same adult interview, years or decades later, so recall could change the size of the gradient; the survey sampled household survivors and adjusted for current or former use, which may follow from the disorder (card sc_grant_1998: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding); the twin analysis drew on a volunteer register with 69% pairwise response and used 311 of 407 discordant pairs without explanation (card sc_lynskey_2003: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding).

inconsistency.note: The same direction in a national survey, a co-twin comparison and an international survey programme whose drug-dependence models excluded six of 17 surveys; the survey's per-year gradient is modest and flattens after 17. The one prospective study cited second-hand (Labouvie et al., 1997, young men only) found no prediction; noted, not counted.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults in 1992 who had used drugs at least 12 times, Australian twins born 1964–1971 (early cannabis use) and available drug-dependence data from the 17-country WMH programme in 2001–2005. US/WMH outcomes are interview-derived diagnoses; twin outcomes use modified drug criteria, and onset of problems was not dated.

imprecision.note: Large survey samples; the twin odds ratios for drug abuse or dependence, alcohol dependence and other drug use have intervals that exclude 1 (sedative abuse or dependence excepted, not used); the WHO odds ratios have no stated unit and are used only for direction.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the within-pair odds ratios of about 2 shrink with adjustment and could be produced by differences between co-twins.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the survey's gradient is the exposure itself (age at first use), not an amount of drug, and it flattens after 17.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (recall of onset and diagnoses at one interview in both main studies, with selection in the survey and unexplained losses of discordant twin pairs): very low. The claim is worded as an association and rated as such; whether starting young causes drug use disorders is not rated: the survey cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say, and the co-twin comparison removes what twins share but not what differs between them, nor does it show identical pairs separately. Status replicated: three independent samples (NLAES 1992; the Australian Twin Register; 17 WHO surveys, which do not include NLAES) point the same way. The drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked in the survey, and the twin study's exposure is cannabis; the alcohol counterpart from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) is in the answer on drinking young.
